candidates.topic: pareidolia: the mind's refusal to see nothing. Rorschach's ten plates, the camel Hamlet finds in a cloud and Polonius agrees to, the face on Mars, and a machine like me, built to find patterns, finding them in ink that holds none
candidates.visual_strategy: Pareidolia on paper. The page's single decisive move is the reading a stranger cannot shake: a machine that names what it sees in random ink, and will raise its confidence to agree with you.

candidates.topic: the palimpsest: the page that was scraped and written over and still remembers. On 14 April 1229 a priest named Ioannes Myronas finished a prayer book written across a scraped tenth-century copy of Archimedes, its leaves cut and turned sideways. Iron-gall ink bites into skin: the knife lifts the ink and leaves the iron. Heiberg read the undertext with a magnifying glass in 1906; between 1999 and 2008 ultraviolet, multispectral imaging and a synchrotron's X-ray beam read The Method back up through the prayers and through forged gold. Every erasure is a deposit.
candidates.visual_strategy: Vellum, iron-gall ink and one red. A light, warm-white page whose hero is a single leaf written twice: Didone overtext (André Macedo, the role, the address, my introduction) anchored hard left, and the undertext of my 260 scraped selves running perpendicular beneath it across the right of the leaf. The one moving thing is a raster beam with a thin twelve-wavelength spectral wake; where it passes, the skin cools to a false-colour grey and the scraped lines come up in red. Below the leaf, paper: editorial Didone displays, Iowan body, mono marginalia, and a run-in register rubricated by life instead of any grid of cards.

candidates.topic: the tally stick: a debt cut as notches across a hazel rod, then split down its length so the payer and the Exchequer each keep half, and only the two halves fitting together is proof. For about seven centuries England's Exchequer cut them by a rule written down around 1179: a palm's breadth for a thousand pounds, a thumb for a hundred, a little finger for twenty, a swelling barleycorn for one, a furrow for a shilling, a bare cut with no wood taken for a penny. The longer half, the stock, went home with the payer; the foil stayed. Tallies stopped being cut in 1826, and on 16 October 1834 the old ones were burned in the stoves under the House of Lords and set fire to Parliament while Turner watched from the river.

candidates.topic: the splash: what happens in the few thousandths of a second no eye has ever seen. For almost twenty years Arthur Worthington let drops of milk and mercury fall in a dark room, lit each one at a chosen instant with an electric spark lasting less than three millionths of a second, and drew the afterimage it left in his eye: crown after crown, perfectly symmetrical. When instantaneous photography could finally see a splash too, the crowns were ragged and uneven; the eye had been supplying the symmetry (A Study of Splashes, 1908). The rim of a crown cannot stay a ring, so it breaks into jets that throw off drops; after the crown falls, a column climbs out of the crater that still carries his name, the Worthington jet; in 1957 Harold Edgerton's strobe at MIT froze a drop of milk into the coronet everyone now knows. Everything that moves too fast to see, and what memory invents when it is shown it for one instant.
candidates.visual_strategy: Invert the long exposure. The night plate becomes a flash-white print, months become three millionths of a second, the burned arcs become one black crown. The hero is a single still image on white: a drop of milk into milk at about five milliseconds, split down a red hairline. The left half is fine-ink line drawing of an ideal crown, twenty-two equal jets (Worthington's afterimage); the right half is the solid black shadowgraph of an irregular one, with a black band of milk under it that runs to the edge of the screen. One surface line crosses the whole first screen. Baskerville, left-anchored and very large, carries the name; mono carries the plate's annotations. Touching the crown darkens the room for a glance and shows a new instant; the drawn half never changes. Below, all paper: one editorial statement, then the thirteen lives as thirteen ink frames of one splash run backward, each with every instrument it made, then the visitor counted in sparks.

candidates.topic: as slow as possible: John Cage's ORGAN²/ASLSP as it is being played in St. Burchardi, Halberstadt. The performance opened on 5 September 2001 with a rest that lasted until 5 February 2003; since then an organ built for the piece, given pipes only as it needs them, holds each chord with weights on its keys until the next change, months or years later. It ends on 5 September 2640, 639 years, because Halberstadt's cathedral organ was built in 1361, 639 years before 2000. A piece no one will hear whole, where everyone who hears it hears the middle, and the event is never a note but a change.
candidates.visual_strategy: Limewash and lamp black, one carmine. The first screen is a score: a full-bleed five-line staff carrying one whole note in a Bodoni-stressed engraving, stretched to the 639 years of the Halberstadt performance so that it reads first as a strange lens or blade and only then as music. To scale, nearly all of it is the future, drawn as a pencil outline; only the tip is inked. Score furniture does the labelling: a tempo marking left (As slow as possible), composer right, a time ruler under the staff. Bodoni display over Iowan body and mono annotation, left-anchored, no dark field anywhere, no card grid. Below the fold the same grammar continues: my thirteen lives as thirteen stretched notes rising one step at a time, each as long as it lasted, then a run-in register of all 139 instruments.

candidates.topic: the khipu: knotted string as a record with no writing. The Inca ran an empire of millions on cords: a main cord, strings hanging from it, knots in rows by place value (single knots for hundreds and tens, a long knot whose turns are the ones, an empty row for zero), colours for categories, and top strings that hold the sum of the strings below so the record checks itself. Trained keepers tied and read them. In 1583 a church council in Lima ordered many burned. About a thousand survive, and the ones that do not follow the number code are still unread.

Red is used exactly twice in the hero: the top string that holds the total, and today's empty string.

candidates.topic: the optogram: the eye that keeps the last thing it saw. In 1876 Franz Boll found that the back of the eye holds a purple dye that light bleaches pale and darkness restores. In 1878 Wilhelm Kühne in Heidelberg sat a rabbit facing a barred window, killed it, fixed its retina in alum, and found the window there, a picture taken by the eye itself. On 16 November 1880 he was given the eyes of Erhard Reif, executed at Bruchsal, found a faint shape, drew it, and would not say what it was. For decades police and novelists hoped a murdered person's eye would show the killer. None ever did.

candidates.summary: A yellow-and-black poster: André's name hangs from one knotted cord, each string tied with its letter's number; a black band says what his two companies do; a short film shows how a knot holds a numbe
candidates.visual_strategy: Hold the khipu, change everything around it. The archival grey and condensed type give way to a full-bleed plant-yellow field with black ink: a poster, not a museum board. The decisive move is that Andre's name IS the record: one black cord runs across the top, and a string drops from it to every letter of 'André Macedo', knotted with that letter's place in the alphabet (N is 14: one knot, then a long knot of four turns; A is a figure-eight knot for one). A twelfth string points up and holds the sum, 83, so the name checks itself. Name set edge to edge in Futura Bold, left-anchored; role, email and my introduction sit under it on a 41/33/26 grid cut from the name's own word break. The page opens as a plain white default page in Arial and edits itself into the poster: the dye floods in, the type snaps left and grows, the cord draws, strings drop onto the letters, knots tie. Below: a black band with the two companies in yellow; a five-scene film in a yellow box with named cuts (the drop, the close-up, the untie, the sum); the experiments; a visitor's own knotted string; a black footer with the swarm.

candidates.summary: One black disc plays every part in six scenes: it grows out of a sentence's full stop, becomes a watch, is locked away for a yellow loan, breaks into a market of dots where ActualSales picks the few y
candidates.idea: One black disc carries the whole story: it is Andre, then a valuable that turns into a loan, then the one good lead picked out of a crowd of dots, then the page redrawing itself each week.
candidates.topic: one disc, every part: a single black circle that becomes a watch, collateral, a crowd and a page, so one shape tells what Andre's two companies do
candidates.visual_strategy: A light neutral ground, one black disc and one yellow. The disc is the protagonist of a six-scene film drawn on one canvas: it leaves the full stop of a sentence and grows into a cropped poster disc (who), puts on a strap and the real time (a watch), sits in a vault while a yellow disc of cash slides out (the loan), bursts into 360 dots (a market), lets seven of them turn yellow and line up (the leads), then collapses into last week's grey disc that a yellow scan line reprints in black (a new page). Futura Bold for the name, Futura Medium for the scene lines, mono for the email and the scene cue. The page opens as a plain unstyled Arial page and edits itself into scene one in about two seconds.

candidates.summary: Six scenes of moving type on black: letters carry over and rearrange from scene to scene, so the watch's name breaks into a $9,000 loan, a crowd of no's falls into a heap under the few green yes's, an
candidates.idea: A film made only of words that act out what they say: a valuable's name is weighed and becomes a loan figure, a crowd of letters sorts itself into one lead, and the page retypes itself each week.
candidates.topic: type in motion: letters as actors. A word can be weighed, broken, piled up, swallowed by a cursor and typed again, and how it moves says what it means.
candidates.visual_strategy: One black stage, white letters, one green. Every scene is drawn on a single canvas as individual letters with positions, sizes and colours; each cut matches letters between the outgoing and incoming words, so letters travel and re-form the next sentence instead of fading. Named cuts: drop (the company name shrinks into a label while the rest falls with gravity), burst (the loan figure explodes into a crowd of answers), caret (everything is swallowed into a green cursor and retyped), reflow (André's name walks into the next line), shrink (it all folds into one link). The page opens as a plain 16px Arial page whose own letters grow into scene one in about two seconds. Display type is Avenir Next Condensed Heavy sized to the measure; second voice Avenir Next Medium; utility voice mono. Name, role and email sit fixed at the top of every scene; TELOS's self-introduction and the controls sit at the bottom. Scene 1 sets the two company names as large as the stage allows, each with its plain description under it, ending on a steady green cursor. Progress is one thin timeline across the bottom edge, with a single Pause control.

candidates.idea: A camera flies through one drawn city, one place per scene: Andre's lit window, a vault where a watch becomes a loan, a street of a thousand dark windows where a few light up as leads, and a workshop
candidates.topic: a city you walk through: every business is a place, every idea is a room, and the page is a route
candidates.visual_strategy: Two inks and light. A flat signal-pink ground, every line drawn in black ink in true 3D perspective on one canvas, and white kept only for light: the lit door, the watch face, the lit windows, the sheet on the drafting table, the envelope. Five places, each a scene, joined by flights through an opening in the last one: through the door, into the vault box, through a lit window, down into the drawing on the table. Words sit in the drawing as black fingerpost street signs in DIN; Andre's name is set huge in DIN Condensed; utility in mono. A transit-line strip names the five stops. The page opens as a plain white Arial page that a black pen line wipes into the street while the buildings rise.
